findings.problem: The section makes the report to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy a personal duty of the pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered. role_duties[9] lists reporting a dispensing error or serious adverse drug event to the Board among the duties of the 'Pharmacist or pharmacy intern after an adverse event', and the other listed fields say the pharmacist or pharmacy intern 'remains responsible for reporting it to the Board'. The Board rule that the circular points to places the report on someone else. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) and (2) the pharmacy's Manager of Record makes both reports. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) puts the duty to report improper dispensing on the pharmacy (it reports to the Department of Public Health), and s. 39D(c) puts the serious-adverse-drug-event report on the manager of record. The section never names the Manager of Record or the pharmacy as the one who files.
findings.rationale: The circular's Reporting Adverse Events section does say the pharmacist or pharmacy intern 'remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board', in accordance with Board regulations. The section reproduces that faithfully and keeps the circular's wording. But the circular's words read most naturally as keeping whatever duty Board regulations already impose, not as creating a new one, and the duty those regulations impose belongs to the Manager of Record. The section turns the sentence into a duty of the person who administers in role_duties, decision_logic and forms_records, and teaches it under learning objective 8 without reconciling it with 247 CMR 20.02. A candidate applying the section to Massachusetts facts would therefore name the administering pharmacist or intern, not the Manager of Record, as the one who must report to the Board. That is a testable actor point, and the cross-reference to the quality-related-events section does not correct it. Repair: keep the circular's sentence, presented as Department guidance. Add that under 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D the report is made by the pharmacy's Manager of Record. Reword role_duties[9] so that it no longer assigns the Board report to the administering pharmacist or intern.

findings.problem: The section says without limit that a dispensing error or a serious adverse drug event following administration 'still has to be reported to the Board under Board regulations' (quick_review[17]), and the other fields treat every such event as reportable to the Board. Board regulations and the statute set narrower triggers. 247 CMR 20.02(1) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) require a report only of improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death. 247 CMR 20.02(2) and s. 39D(c) require a serious-adverse-drug-event report only for a drug manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. Both reports run on a seven-business-day clock, which the section does not mention.
findings.rationale: 'Under Board regulations' does not tell the candidate that those regulations limit the report, so the quick review and the decision logic read as an unconditional rule. On Massachusetts facts, a candidate would wrongly conclude that two kinds of event must be reported to the Board. One is a dispensing error that causes only a minor reaction: 247 CMR 20.02(1) does not reach it, because the error did not result in serious injury or death. The other is a serious adverse drug event, with no error, from one of the commercially manufactured injectables on the list: 247 CMR 20.02(2) does not reach it, because the drug was not manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. worked_examples[4] can keep its result once the actor is corrected, because a wrong product that leads to an inpatient admission is the kind of event 247 CMR 20.02(1) addresses. Repair: make the Board report conditional on what Board regulations require, and state the triggers and the seven-business-day clock, or name them and point to the quality-related-events section.

findings.problem: The entry says the circular's list supplies 'the specific drugs that 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d)1. requires the Department's guidelines to address'. Paragraph (d)1. concerns the specific drugs permitted to be administered under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), and (B)(9) reaches only FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs. The list's testosterone, HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection entries are not (B)(9) drugs.
findings.rationale: Read alone, the sentence could suggest that the whole list, testosterone and the HIV prevention and STI medications included, is administered under (B)(9). Elsewhere the section says the opposite plainly (orientation[4]; common_traps[7] and [8]), so a candidate is unlikely to be misled, and the severity is Low. Repair: say that the list supplies the (d)1. specific drugs for the mental health and substance use disorder categories, and also lists the categories that line up with clauses (c)(ii) and (c)(iii) of the statutory definition.

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, Medium. I checked the section field by field against the current official texts. Almost everything is accurate. The three pharmacist routes in clause (c) of the definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, and what gates each one, are right. So is the pharmacist's s. 9(a) entry 'as limited by' s. 7(g) and c. 112, s. 24B1/2, with the possession limb and the administration limb. Also right: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), from its heading through (a)-(d), (d)1.-9. and (e); (B)(6), with its 5-or-older floor, practitioner order and disclosure and cost notice; and 700.003(F) (all read in the current Mass. Register #1514 PDF). Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 is presented as Department guidance, and its requirements are stated accurately, each with the circular's own modality: the list, the 18-or-older condition, the MCSR point, reassessment, SC/IM only and not intravenous, single-dose packaging with refills allowed, training, CPR, competency, counseling, the pharmacy's record, 'should' within 24 hours versus 'must' immediately, privacy, and the notation and communication section, where every sentence is hortatory. The section's reading that the eligible list closes only the circular's own pathway is sound: the circular's Purpose and its methadone NOTE support it, and a guidance list cannot displace (B)(6), (B)(9)(e) or 700.003(F). Its reading of the NOTE as governing administration by order is the reading the circular's own listing of long-acting injectable buprenorphine and naltrexone requires. Its safe courses (age, route, dose and packaging, and interns on the OTP route) are safe. The federal statements match 21 CFR 1306.07(a) and (d), with methadone in Schedule II. 1306.04(c) confirms that no Schedule II maintenance prescription is provided for, and 1306.07(b) and (c) give no prescription or pharmacy route, so the conclusions stand. All six practice questions (MA-Q-0330, 0331, 0332, 0356, 0359, 0423) are answerable from the section and are not contradicted by it. The defect is in the Board-reporting teaching. Following the circular's wording, the section makes the administering pharmacist or intern responsible for reporting to the Board and says a dispensing error or serious adverse drug event 'still has to be reported'. 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D place the report on the Manager of Record (s. 39D(b): the pharmacy). They require it only for improper dispensing resulting in serious injury or death, or a serious adverse drug event from a drug made or compounded at the pharmacy, within seven business days. One Low paraphrase issue in forms_records[11] ((d)1.) is noted.
